links.note: In 1321 the woman says he has no fault (இல்லை தவறவர்க்கு), yet the way he shows tenderness (அவர் அளிக்குமாறு) is able to produce a sulk. In 1325 the man says that even when men are faultless (தவறிலர் ஆயினும்), being kept from the soft arms of the one they love 'has a certain something' (ஆங்கொன்று உடைத்து). The chapter opens each speaker's side with the same concession: the sulk it praises needs no offence.

In 1311 the woman refuses his chest because all women 'feast on it in common with their eyes' (கண்ணின் பொதுஉண்பர்), a sulk with a stated ground. In 1321 she grants there is no fault at all and says his tenderness itself brings the sulk on; Parimelazhagar explains this as her thought that others too might receive that same tenderness. On his reading the jealousy of 1311 survives in 1321 with its ground removed.

Both verses use the rare word சிறுதுனி for a brief bad spell in something good. In 1010 the short want of the renowned rich is like the rain-cloud going dry (மாரி வறங்கூர்ந்தனையது); in 1322 the small pain that sulking brings may make his good tenderness droop (நல்லளி வாடினும்), yet it gains worth (பாடு பெறும்). In each the dryness is temporary and belongs to a giver whose giving is not in doubt.

1306 says love without துனி and புலவி is like fruit over-ripe or unripe (கனியும் கருக்காயும் அற்று), so some quarrel is needed. 1322 names the amount: only the 'small துனி' that arises in a sulk (ஊடலின் தோன்றும் சிறுதுனி), which leaves his tenderness greater even if it droops for a while. Parimelazhagar on 1306 takes துனி as the full-grown quarrel and புலவி as the young one, so 1322's சிறு marks the tolerable dose.

1322 says tenderness may wilt (வாடினும்) under the small pain of a sulk and still come to greatness. 1304 uses the same verb for the limit: not reconciling one who has sulked is like cutting an already wilted creeper at the root (வாடிய வள்ளி முதலரிந்தற்று). The wilting is harmless only if the sulk is ended; Parimelazhagar reads 1304 as the woman speaking of his other women.

1103 asks whether the world of the lotus-eyed one (தாமரைக் கண்ணான் உலகு) is as sweet as sleeping on the soft arms of the one you love. 1323 asks whether there is a land of the gods (புத்தேள்நாடு உண்டோ) like sulking with one joined to you as water to earth. The man's question at the first union and the woman's at the end of the book have the same form, and the thing set above heaven has moved from the embrace to the quarrel.

452 says water changes by the nature of the land it meets (நிலத்தியல்பால் நீர் திரிந்தற்று), and so a person's understanding takes the nature of their company. 1323 describes lovers as joined like water with land (நிலத்தொடு நீர் இயைந்தன்னார்). Parimelazhagar explains 1323 with the logic of 452, that water becomes of the nature of the ground it stands on, so the image that warns against bad company in 452 here describes a complete union.

1309 says water is sweet only in the shade, and sulking is sweet only with those who love (புலவியும் வீழுநர் கண்ணே இனிது). 1323 says the sulk that surpasses heaven is the one with those joined like water and earth (நிலத்தொடு நீர் இயைந்தன்னார் அகத்து). Both verses, each with a water image, put the sweetness of sulking under the same condition: it holds only where the bond is already secure.

In 1258 the woman calls her lover's humble words (பணிமொழி) 'the weapon that breaks our womanhood' (பெண்மை உடைக்கும் படை). 1324 says that within the sulk arises 'the weapon that breaks my heart' (என் உள்ளம் உடைக்கும் படை) and does not name it; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both gloss it as humble words, Parimelazhagar adding bowing. 1258 supplies the identity of the weapon that 1324 leaves unstated, though the commentators differ on whether the woman or the man speaks 1324.

828 warns that a weapon lies hidden inside an enemy's hands folded in worship (தொழுதகையுள்ளும் படையொடுங்கும்), and his tears are the same. 1324 finds a weapon (படை) inside the lovers' sulk, which Parimelazhagar explains as the other's bowing and humble words. Submission as a concealed weapon is a danger to be detected in false friendship and, in love, the means by which the sulk is ended.

1251 says the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint bolted with shame (காமக் கணிச்சி உடைக்கும் நிறையென்னும் ... கதவு). 1324 uses the same verb for the resolve to keep sulking: a weapon arises that breaks the heart (உள்ளம் உடைக்கும் படை). What was a breach forced during separation in 1251 becomes, inside the sulk, a breaking that leads to the embrace that does not let go (புல்லி விடா).

Both verses turn on the same phrase, 'the soft arms of the one they love' (தாம்வீழ்வார் மென்றோள்). In 1103 sleeping on them is set against the world of the lotus-eyed one; in 1325 being kept away from them (அகறலின்), though one is faultless, 'has a certain something' (ஆங்கொன்று உடைத்து). The repeated phrase shows the book's last chapter finding a pleasure in the very absence of what the first union praised.

1325 says that being kept from her arms by a sulk has a pleasure of its own (ஆங்கொன்று உடைத்து). 1307 says sulking also holds one pain: the thought of whether union will be delayed or not (புணர்வது நீடுவது அன்றுகொல் என்று). Parimelazhagar gives both to the man, 1325 after the making up and 1307 during the sulk, so the pleasure of 1325 is one judged in hindsight.

In 1319 the man reports that even when he tries to appease her she is angry (உணர்த்தினும் காயும்), saying he is like this with others too: a complaint that he is blamed without cause. In 1325 he grants the same situation, a man without fault (தவறிலர் ஆயினும்) kept from her arms, and finds something to enjoy in it. The groundless sulks listed in chapter 132 are re-read as a pleasure in chapter 133.

944 instructs: know that the earlier meal is digested (அற்றது அறிந்து) and eat only when thoroughly hungry (துவரப் பசித்து). 1326 says the digesting of what was eaten is sweeter than eating (உணலினும் உண்டது அறல் இனிது), and so sulking is sweeter than union. The chapter on medicine states as a rule of health what the man uses as his simile; Parimelazhagar on 1326 draws the same line, that one who eats when hungry eats more and with more relish.

1326 ranks sulking above union: ஊடல் is sweeter than புணர்தல் for love. 1330 calls sulking love's pleasure but adds that the pleasure of the sulk itself lies in being able to come together and embrace (கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின்). The closing verse makes the sulk's sweetness depend on the union that 1326 placed below it, as digestion has value for the next meal.

986 says the touchstone of worth is to accept defeat even from those who are not one's equals (தோல்வி துலையல்லார் கண்ணும் கொளல்). 1327 says that in a sulk those who lost have won (ஊடலில் தோற்றவர் வென்றார்), which is seen in the union that follows. Accepting defeat is a test of character in 986 and the winning move in 1327; Parimelazhagar glosses the loser of 1327 as the one who gave way, unable to keep opposing.

931 says not to want gambling even if you win, since what is won (வென்றதூஉம்) is like the hook a fish has swallowed. 1327 says that in a sulk the loser is the winner (தோற்றவர் வென்றார்). The two verses reverse the apparent result of a contest in opposite directions: the gambler's win is a loss that shows later, and the lover's loss is a win that shows later in union (கூடலிற் காணப்படும்).

1302 says sulking is like salt in the right amount (உப்பு அமைந்தற்றால் புலவி), and prolonging it is like a little too much. 1328 calls the pleasure of the union that follows a sulk its உப்பு, the savour that appeared in union with her forehead sweating, and asks whether sulking will win it again. Salt is the sulk as seasoning in 1302 and the resulting savour in 1328; Parimelazhagar glosses 1328's உப்பு as sweetness.

802 says intimate liberty is a limb of friendship and that 'being உப்பு to it' (அதற்கு உப்பாதல்) is the duty of the worthy; Parimelazhagar reads this as being pleasant toward that liberty. 1328 uses உப்பு for the savour of union after a sulk, which Parimelazhagar again glosses as sweetness. In both, salt stands for the relish that makes something a close companion does, a liberty or a sulk, enjoyable and not an offence.

In 1238 the man recalls that when he loosened the arms that embraced her, her forehead turned pale (பசந்தது ... பேதை நுதல்). In 1328 he recalls union so intense that her forehead sweated (நுதல் வெயர்ப்ப). Her forehead is the place where he reads both the first sign of separation and the fullness of union.

In 1169 the separated woman says the nights that now pass so long (நெடிய கழியும் இரா) are crueller than the cruelty of the man who left. In 1329 the man wishes the night to lengthen (நீடுக மன்னோ இரா) so that he may go on pleading while she sulks. The long night is the worst of separation in her mouth and a wish in his, once the lovers are together and the only distance is a sulk.

1307 names the one pain within sulking: the thought of whether union will be delayed or not (புணர்வது நீடுவது அன்றுகொல்). 1329 wishes for that delay, asking that she keep sulking and the night grow long (ஊடுக ... நீடுக). Parimelazhagar gives both to the man, 1307 during a sulk and 1329 after one has ended well, so the delay feared in the moment is desired in retrospect.

1052 says even begging is a pleasure to a person if what is begged for comes without pain (இன்பம் ஒருவற்கு இரத்தல்). In 1329 the man wants the sulk and the night prolonged so that he may beg (யாம் இரப்ப), treating the pleading itself as something to enjoy. Begging, which chapter 107 calls degrading, is here a pleasure because the giver is not in doubt, which is the condition 1052 sets.

1109 lists sulking, reconciling and uniting (ஊடல் உணர்தல் புணர்தல்) as the gains of those joined in love. 1330, the last verse of the book, orders the same elements: sulking is the pleasure of love, and the pleasure of sulking is to come together and embrace (கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின்). What 1109 gives as a list early in the Book of Love, 1330 states as a dependence of each step on the next.

1330 says the sulk's own pleasure comes if the lovers get to unite and embrace (பெறின்). 1304 states the other case: not reconciling one who has sulked (ஊடியவரை உணராமை) is like cutting a wilted creeper at the root. The conditional in 1330 is a real one, and 1304 shows what a sulk is when the condition fails.

1302 says a sulk is like salt in the right amount, and letting it run long (நீள விடல்) is like a little too much. 1330 makes the sulk love's pleasure only if embrace follows (கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின்). Parimelazhagar reads 1330's condition through this measure: the sulk must be ended at the right point, between a quarrel too ripe and one too young, and that is hard to judge.
